content.text: Mentorship and practice develop skill and connect individuals to their community and heritage.
Through practice and mentorship, people turn skill into voice and work into art.
In Lesson 34, students will begin collecting and organizing text evidence from
A Single Shard
about the stages of learning.
This lesson has students work collaboratively with peers to generate and organize ideas in preparation for research and writing.
A Single Shard
by Linda Sue Park
Unit 2 Lesson 33 Student Edition
Research Notes graphic organizer
Teacher search: Short video about Goryeo celadon pottery

Directions:
Make connections to what you have learned about finding and integrating evidence to support a research topic.
Read the following prompts related to the stages of learning.

Reflection
How confident do you feel about your ability to gather sources and evidence when researching an explanatory essay?

Choose a number between 1 and 5, with 1 being the least confident and 5 being the most confident, to rate your confidence level. Then write a sentence explaining how you can better understand this skill.
Part B: On-Demand Writing
Directions:
Write two body paragraphs to respond to your chosen prompt using the sources and evidence you have gathered.
Body Paragraph Checklist:

Evidence that supports the main idea or claim
Analysis that explains how the evidence connects to the main idea or claim
A concluding sentence that connects the text evidence and analysis to the topic sentence
Requirements:

Use multiple sources.

Checklist
Make sure to:
☐ Gather evidence from two sources relevant to your prompt.
☐ Write two body paragraphs to answer the prompt.

Quick Write
Directions:
Write a one- to two-sentence response to the following prompt:
How do you know if a source or piece of evidence is relevant to your research?
Turn and Talk
Unpack students’ prior knowledge of the stages of learning.
Say These Directions:
Turn and Talk
to respond to the following questions.
Ask:
How has
A Single Shard
shaped what we know about the stages of learning?
A Single Shard

has shaped what we know about the stages of learning by showing the different steps that Tree-ear has taken to learn the craft of pottery making. Through the novel, he has observed, tried, failed, refined, and created.
Ask:
What other sources have we explored that support these ideas?

Other sources that support these ideas include the article “Hands That Remember: Artists Who Make Things by Hand”, the video about Korean pottery, the video about boot making, and the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive.”
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, we’ll continue our discussion of the stages of learning by gathering sources and evidence related to a research question about one or more of the stages and their connection to apprenticeship.
Students will use the Turn and Talk routine to reflect on how
A Single Shard
has shaped their understanding of the stages of learning.
Gathering Sources and Evidence for Research
Say:
Throughout Unit 2, you have explored the stages of learning, mentorship, and apprenticeship in a variety of texts, including the novel
A Single Shard
and several informational articles and videos. During the Performance Task, you will use these sources to help you write an explanatory essay about the stages of learning.
Share with students the following prompts related to the stages of learning.
What role does observation play in apprenticeship?
How do apprentices benefit from trying and failing?
How do apprenticeships help learners refine their skills over time?
How are creating and mastery related to apprenticeship and mentorship?
Discuss the steps of gathering sources and evidence for research.
Say:

Gathering sources and evidence is an important part of the research process. It helps us determine and organize which details and information we will include in our writing. Today, you will be gathering sources and evidence to answer one of these questions. Use these questions to guide you.
What question am I answering?
I’m going to respond to the first prompt: What role does observation play in apprenticeship?
What information do I need to answer the question?
I’ll need evidence related to the observation stage of learning and how it is connected to apprenticeship and mentorship.
Which sources from the unit include evidence to answer the prompt?
The novel
A Single Shard
includes many examples of Tree-ear observing Min and other potters. The video about the boot-making apprenticeship also shows the observation stage of learning.
Say These Directions:
Use a
Research Notes
graphic organizer to gather evidence.
Model how to complete the graphic organizer using evidence from the sources you’ve identified.
Say:
Now that I’ve identified my sources, I’ll use the
Research Notes
graphic organizer to help me gather evidence. I’ll start by adding the prompt to the Research Question/Topic box at the top. Then I’ll add
A Single Shard
(source 1) and the boot-making video (source 2) to the column on the left.
As a class, identify evidence from the two sources to populate the fact boxes. Then model how to summarize the findings.
Say:

After I’ve gathered my sources and evidence, I should summarize my findings. When we summarize our findings, we look for big ideas or takeaways from the evidence we’ve gathered and how they relate to our research question or topic.
Research question/topic:
What role does observation play in apprenticeship?
Source 1:
A Single Shard
Fact 1:
Tree-ear observes Min making pottery, which piques his interest in learning the craft. (pp. 10–13)
Fact 2:
Tree-ear observes how other potters cut clay from the riverbank, an important skill needed for making pottery at this time. (pp. 31–33)
Fact 3:
Tree-ear observes how Min tests the clay to see if it has been refined enough to be used, which helps him understand why the clay must be purified. (p. 42)
Source 2:
Boot-making video
Fact 1:
The apprentice watches as the master boot maker uses different tools and models different skills.
Fact 2:
The apprentice takes detailed notes, makes illustrations, and takes photos of the boot-making process.
Fact 3:
The apprentice uses her notes to review different steps and to help other learners.
Summary of findings:
During the observation phase, learners study what masters are doing. By observing, they gain knowledge about how and why things are done before applying this knowledge on their own.
Help students learn how to select sources and record evidence for a research question by rehearsing ideas aloud using tentative academic language and clarifying questions before they write.
Validate multiple valid source pairings (novel + video, novel + poem, two informational sources) as long as students can explain relevance.
Model “research talk” as non-final: use hedging on purpose (e.g., “It might be that . . .” / “One possibility is . . .”).
Name the 3 decisions explicitly while modeling: Which prompt? Which 2 sources? Which 3 facts from each source?
Require students to add a Source Reason line after each source: “This source fits because . . .”
Build a quick “clarify first” routine: ask one question before locking in evidence.
“One possibility is that ___ because ___.”
“It might be that ___; another possibility is ___.”
“Can you clarify which detail shows ___?”
“Where in the source do you see that (page/scene/section)?”
Revoice certainty into appropriate tentativeness: “This proves . . .” → “This suggests . . .”
Press for alignment: “It’s relevant” → “It’s relevant because it answers ___ in the prompt.”
Upgrade vague evidence: “Tree-ear learned” → “Tree-ear learned by observing ___ (what/where), which suggests ___.”
If students pick sources without explaining fit → Prompt: “Add ‘This source fits because it helps answer . . .’”
If evidence is a summary only → Prompt: “Name one specific moment/detail, and say what it suggests.”
Students use at least one tentative stem accurately during discussion.
Students ask at least one clarification question before finalizing evidence.
Research notes include prompt and 2 sources and 2–3 facts per source (with location/page/scene when possible).
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:

Today, you’ll apply the skill of gathering sources and evidence with a small group to answer one of the prompts about the stages of learning. Gathering sources and evidence will help you as you prepare to work on your Performance Task essay starting in Lesson 34.
Students will observe as the teacher models how to gather resources and evidence for research.
Part A: Select a Prompt and Gather Sources and Evidence (W.6.7, W.6.9) (10 minutes)
Organize the class into small groups of three or four students and distribute the Research Notes organizer.
Say These Directions:

Choose one of the prompts about the stages of learning. Work with your group to identify two sources that will help you answer the question. Then gather evidence from each source. Identify the page number or use exact quotes as needed. Record your responses in the
Research Notes
graphic organizer.
Invite two or three groups to share their responses with the class.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Gathering Sources and Evidence

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Identifying relevant sources and evidence

Provide students with sentence frames to help them explain why they have selected their sources and evidence. (Ex. “This source answers the question by ____.” “This source shows that ____.” “This piece of evidence suggests ____.”)
Ready for extension: Conducting outside research
Invite students to identify other texts not explored during the unit that answer their selected prompt. These may be other novels, media, or informational articles.
Reflection (W.6.7, W.6.9)
Reflect on your understanding of gathering sources and evidence using the Reflection routine.
How confident do you feel about your ability to gather sources and evidence when researching an explanatory essay?
Then write a sentence explaining how you can better understand this skill.
Support groups in choosing a prompt and gathering evidence efficiently by using oral rehearsal to test relevance and by asking clarification questions to refine ideas.
Encourage students to bring in lived experiences of learning (sports, music, art, gaming) as talk rehearsal while keeping written evidence anchored to sources.
Require a 90-second “prompt pitch” in groups before filling the organizer: “We chose ___ because . . .”
Set team roles: Clarifier (must ask two questions), Evidence Finder (must locate details), Recorder (must write facts in organizer).
Have groups label each fact with a stage of learning (observe, try, fail, refine, create) to keep evidence aligned.
“Our prompt is ___. One possibility is that ___.”
“Can you clarify how this detail connects to the stage of ___?”
“This evidence suggests ___, so it supports our prompt by ___.”
Revoice weak alignment: “This is about learning” → “This connects to refining because . . .”
Push justification connectors: “We picked it” → “We picked it because it shows ___, so it helps answer ___.”
Tighten evidence language: “It says” → “The text/video explains/notes/describes . . .”
If groups collect too many facts with no focus → Prompt: “Star your best three facts per source—the ones that most directly answer the prompt.”
If groups can’t agree → Prompt: “Choose the prompt that you can support with the clearest evidence from two sources.”
Groups can state the prompt and explain why their sources fit using because language.
Each source has at least two facts that clearly connect to the prompt.
Students use at least one clarification question to improve evidence selection.
Part B: On-Demand Writing (W.6.7, W.6.9) (20 minutes)
After students have finished gathering sources and evidence, have them work independently to write two body paragraphs to answer their chosen prompt.
Say These Directions:
Work independently to write two body paragraphs to respond to your chosen prompt using the sources and evidence you have gathered in your organizer. Make sure to include the elements listed below.
Display the
Body Paragraph Checklist:
A topic sentence that states the main idea or claim of the paragraph
Evidence that supports the main idea or claim
Analysis that explains how the evidence connects to the main idea or claim
A concluding sentence that connects the text evidence and analysis to the topic sentence
Display the
Requirements:
Include four or five sentences per paragraph
Use multiple sources
Use at least two academic connectors (because, therefore, as a result)
Scoring Rubric:
1 – Developing
2 – Approaching
3 – Meets
Components of a body paragraph
Student includes only one or two components of a body paragraph.
Student includes three of the components of a body paragraph.
Student includes all four components of a body paragraph.
Integration of evidence
Student does not use any evidence or cites irrelevant evidence.
Student cites some evidence relevant to the topic sentence but does not fully explain the evidence.
Student fully integrates evidence to make connections to the topic sentence and their ideas.
Punctuation and conventions
Student uses little to no punctuation or uses punctuation incorrectly. Student does not follow accepted writing conventions.
Student uses punctuation throughout the paragraph with some errors. Student follows accepted writing conventions with some errors.
Student uses accurate punctuation and follows accepted writing conventions with few or no errors.
Language
Student does not use transitional words or phrases to connect ideas. Student consistently uses the incorrect pronoun case.
Student uses some transitional words and phrases to connect ideas. Student occasionally uses the correct pronoun case.
Student successfully uses transitional words and phrases to connect evidence to the topic sentence and to their analysis. Student successfully uses the correct pronoun case throughout the paragraph.
Help students turn research notes into two clear body paragraphs by using rehearsed ideas, tentative academic language (when appropriate), and clear evidence-to-idea links.
Allow students to choose the prompt that matches their interests (pottery, boot making, poems) to increase ownership and idea fluency.
Give a paragraph template that mirrors the task:
Require students to add one sentence of reasoning after each fact: “This suggests . . .” / “This shows . . .”
Quick oral rehearsal before writing: students say their topic sentence + best fact aloud to a partner.
“One possibility is that ___ because the source describes ___.”
“This detail suggests ___, so it supports the prompt by ___.”
“A clarifying question I answered in my writing is ___.”
Paragraph 1: topic sentence → 2–3 facts (from at least 2 sources) → explanation → concluding sentence
Paragraph 2: topic sentence → 2–3 facts (from at least 2 sources) → explanation → concluding sentence
Convert lists into analysis: “First, . . . Second, . . .” → add “This suggests . . .” after each.
Strengthen academic caution when needed: “This proves apprenticeships always . . .” → “This suggests apprenticeships often . . .”
Upgrade connectors for logic: and → as a result/therefore/because/for this reason.
If paragraph is summary-only → Prompt: “Add one sentence starting with ‘This suggests . . .’ explaining why the detail matters.”
If topic sentence repeats the prompt with no stance → Prompt: “Add a claim word: shows/explains/demonstrates.”
If evidence is vague → Prompt: “Replace it with the specific noun (Tree-ear/Min/the apprentice/the craft).”
Each paragraph includes: topic sentence + evidence + explanation + concluding sentence.
Students use at least two academic connectors (because/therefore/as a result).
Students use at least one tentative academic stem appropriately when making a broad claim.
Writing clearly answers the chosen prompt using evidence from both sources.

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Writing topic sentences
Model how to write a topic sentence by restating the prompt. (Ex. “The novel
A Single Shard
shows how apprentices benefit from trying and failing in several ways.” “The novel
A Single Shard
shows that apprenticeships help learners refine their skills over time by giving them multiple opportunities to test their abilities.”)
Ready for extension: Comparing sources
Ask:
How are the ideas in the sources you’ve gathered similar and different? Why is it important to gather diverse sources when conducting research? The ideas in
A Single Shard

show a fictional version of the actual stages of learning, while the boot-making video shows how a modern apprentice applies the stages of learning today. Gathering diverse sources helps writers create a stronger foundation for their essays and makes it easier for them to support their ideas when answering a research question.
Checklist (W.6.7, W.6.9)
You will turn in your body paragraphs for feedback. A strong draft should:
☐ Gather evidence from two sources relevant to your chosen prompt.
☐ Write two body paragraphs to answer the prompt.
☐ Integrate evidence from your sources.
☐ Analyze or explain the evidence you chose.
☐ Include all components of a body paragraph in your writing.
Part A: Select a Prompt and Gather Sources and Evidence (W.6.7, W.6.9)
Students will work with a partner to gather sources and evidence related to a self-selected prompt about the stages of learning.
Part B: On-Demand Writing (W.6.7, W.6.9)
Students will work independently to write two body paragraphs in response to their self-selected prompt using the sources and evidence they have gathered.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Respond to the following

prompt in one or two sentences.
Ask:
How do you know if a source or piece of evidence is relevant to your research?
I know a source or piece of evidence is relevant to my research if it is related to or helps answer my research question or topic.
Students will respond to a Quick Write prompt reflecting on how they know if the sources and evidence they have gathered are relevant.
